Is the following result in mathlib? I'm surprised I couldn't find it anywhere. inferInstance doesn't work, either.

example {α : Type*} : Monoid (List α) where
  mul := (· ++ ·)
  mul_assoc := List.append_assoc
  one := []
  one_mul := List.nil_append
  mul_one := List.append_nil
see docs#FreeMonoid
Thanks! But where is it proved that a FreeMonoid is a Monoid?
https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/FreeMonoid/Basic.html#FreeMonoid.instCancelMonoid
Ah, I see. Thanks!

But, still, CancelMonoid (FreeMonoid α) implies Monoid (FreeMonoid α), not Monoid (List α) or CancelMonoid (List α). To be sure, FreeMonoid α and List α are Equiv, but that falls short of saying that they are isomorphic as monoids, doesn't it? If I want to use List α as a monoid, I still have to prove it manually, don't I?
Why do you want to use List as a monoid?
Does it have to be specifically List for some reason? Why can't you just use FreeMonoid instead?

Because I want to talk about homomorphism between languages (in the CS sense):
https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Computability/Language.html
which are defined on List α. Computer scientists talk about lists, not free monoids!
Can you elaborate on where the need for the Monoid structure shows up?
I want to prove that the image and inverse image of a regular language are still regular under a "homomorphism", which is really a monoid homomorphism when List α is viewed as a monoid.
Here's the definition of a "homomorphism" from Dexter Kozen's textbook:
It is a monoid homomorphism, isn't it?
I don't mind proving Monoid (List α) myself, but it seems rather strange that this result is not in mathlib already.

Since a homomorphism is exactly determined by its action on the singletons could you maybe just take an ordinary function Σ→Γ∗\Sigma \to \Gamma^*Σ→Γ∗? The action on lists is given by docs#List.flatMap.
That's not the most natural definition, when we have the perfectly good monoid homomorphism notion to use.
There is an open PR to redefine Language in terms of FreeMonoid, at which point you wouldn't need to talk about List

What is that PR?

I'm not sure that's a good idea. Language is mostly used by computer scientists and most computer scientists are not taught what a "free monoid" is. Defining Language in terms of FreeMonoid just creates confusion without adding anything of mathematical substance. Indeed, if you look at the code of FreeMonoid, it's literally just an alias for List:
https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/b78b57f2047c2f441a7ce779a951cd9db0258a6d/Mathlib/Algebra/FreeMonoid/Basic.lean#L65-L66
and most theorems in that file are proved using theorems about List (or literally direct translations of theorems about List). Furthermore, why stop at Language? Why not change List to FreeMonoid everywhere?
IMHO, if you want to improve mathlib's Language, you should get the PR mathlib#36934 merged first. That PR has been open for 5 months and actually does something meaningful.

Well the problem is that there is not just one reasonable Monoid structure on Lists. For example, you could also consider elementwise multiplication as a monoid where (1 : List Nat) = [1] and [2, 6] * [3, 4] = [6, 8, 18, 24]. Furthermore, you might want to instead have an additive structure on lists and if we had both it would be even more confusing. Instead, if you want lists with concatenation as multiplication / addition, you should use FreeMonoid / FreeAddMonoid.

@Ching-Tsun Chou I agree with the other messages in the thread: this is a common idiom whenever there are multiple reasonable instances for the same type. It's analogous to why we have both Monoid and AddMonoid. Imagine the confusion if these were combined and one class needed to handle both the additive and multiplicative cases for say the natural numbers. It may also be desirable for FreeMonoid to be a one-field structure, but this is an independent issue.

My problem is how do I define a "homomorphism" between languages by leveraging the monoid structure of List under ++ and []. The most straightforward approach that occurs to me is to prove Monoid (List α) (or the stronger CancelMonoid (List α) and then say a "homomorphism" is a monoid homomorphism under this monoid structure. But I seem to be told that this is not a good idea. I don't really understand why this is not a good idea. That there is an alternative monoid structure on List doesn't mean Monoid (List α) is not true, does it? (Indeed, my example at the beginning proves it.) Why can't I use a true fact?
Another approach is to just define a "homomorphism" exactly as in Dexter Kozen's textbook without pointing out the connection to monoids at all. But is that a good idea?

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

That there is an alternative monoid structure on List doesn't mean Monoid (List α) is not true, does it? (Indeed, my example at the beginning proves it.) Why can't I use a true fact?

Monoid (List α) is not a proposition, so it can't be true or false. It is true that Nonempty (Monoid (List α)), but that probably doesn't help you.

I don't understand the opposition to FreeMonoid, but you can probably have a def for Monoid (List α) using concatenation, or perhaps a scoped instance.

e.g.

import Mathlib
@[implicit_reducible]
def List.appendCancelMonoid (α : Type*) : CancelMonoid (List α) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| CancelMonoid (FreeMonoid α)

@Snir Broshi I'm not opposed to FreeMonoid. I just don't know how it can help me if I'm not even supposed to talk about Monoid (List α) or CancelMonoid (List α). At least that's my impression from reading the comments above. If my impression is wrong, please let me know. It's not hard to prove CancelMonoid (List α) even without using FreeMonoid.

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

I'm not even supposed to talk about Monoid (List α) or CancelMonoid (List α)

If you create a def or a scoped instance then I think it's fine. But creating a global instance for it would mean that you're forcing a specific choice of Monoid on lists for whoever imports your code, which isn't great.

For (Σ Γ : Type*) you can talk about FreeMonoid Σ →* FreeMonoid Γ, which is the type of monoid homomorphisms from List Σ to List Γ where the monoid action on both sides is appending lists.
Right now FreeMonoid is a "type-alias" for Lists (as you've noticed), so everything works great.
If Mathlib decides that lists are an implementation detail then they might change the definition of FreeMonoid at any point, so using it might not be a good idea, but I think strings in CS are free monoids, so even if the underlying representation changes you're good.

I think you can either:

  • Use FreeMonoid α
  • Create your own type-alias for Lists and define a global instance : CancelMonoid (Foo α)
  • Create a scoped instance : CancelMonoid (List α)

All 3 are probably fine, and the 3rd option is probably easiest to understand since there's no type-alias involved.
The difference is semantics: are you really working with lists, or with a free monoid that just happens to be implemented by lists (but could be e.g. String, or a custom structure containing a list), or with something else entirely?

one compromise could be defining your own type of "language homomorphisms", which under the hood are monoid homs but come with a FunLike instance on lists

def LanguageHom (α β : Type*) : Type* :=
    FreeMonoid α →* FreeMonoid β

instance (α β : Type*) : FunLike (LanguageHom α β) (List α) (List β) where
  ...

not sure if that addresses your concerns

What is the difference between MonoidHom and MonoidHomClass in mathlib?
Never mind. I figured that out.

Using @Thomas Waring's idea, I got the following code, which seems quite nice:

namespace Language

open FreeMonoid

variable {α β : Type*}

abbrev Hom (α β : Type*) := FreeMonoid α →* FreeMonoid β

scoped instance : FunLike (Hom α β) (List α) (List β) where
  coe (f : Hom α β) := toList ∘ f ∘ ofList
  coe_injective := by
    intro _ _ h
    ext a
    exact funext_iff.mp h [a]

namespace Hom

variable (f : Hom α β)

theorem map_one : f [] = [] := by
  exact MonoidHom.map_one f

theorem map_mul (as as' : List α) : f (as ++ as') = (f as) ++ (f as') := by
  exact MonoidHom.map_mul f as as'

end Hom

end Language

After playing with the above code more, I think it doesn't really work. For example, it doesn't allow me to define the function lift below. I realized that I actually don't need to show that Monoid (List α) or use FreeMonoid α, because of the very extensive set of results already proved for List in mathlib. So the following code should suffice for my purpose. I do need to introduce instances of One and Mul for List, but I've limited its scope to the namespace Language.

namespace Language

variable {α β : Type*}

scoped instance : MulOne (List α) where
  one := []
  mul := (· ++ ·)

def Hom (α β : Type*) := MonoidHom (List α) (List β)

namespace Hom

theorem map_one (f : List α →* List β) : f [] = [] := by
  exact MonoidHom.map_one f

theorem map_mul (f : List α →* List β) (as as' : List α) :
    f (as ++ as') = (f as) ++ (f as') := by
  exact MonoidHom.map_mul f as as'

def lift (f : α → List β) : List α →* List β where
  toFun := List.flatMap f
  map_one' := List.flatMap_nil
  map_mul' := fun _ _ ↦ List.flatMap_append

end Hom

end Language

Yaël Dillies said:

There is an open PR to redefine Language in terms of FreeMonoid, at which point you wouldn't need to talk about List

Was this SetSemiring (FreeMonoid A)?

I'd like to observe that Language needs to support a much richer structure than just semirings. For example, regular languages are closed under reversal, intersection, complementation, and Kleene star. None of those operations are available in a semirings.
Is there any reason to believe these couldn't be implemented on docs#SetSemiring ? Type synonyms are useful to distinguish disagreeing instances, but they can otherwise copy the other instances

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

For example, it doesn't allow me to define the function lift below.

this needn't necessarily change your decision, but defining lift is exactly what FreeMonoid is built for, viz

import Mathlib

variable {α β : Type*}

abbrev LanguageHom (α β : Type*) := FreeMonoid α →* FreeMonoid β

@[simps]
instance instFunlikeLanguageHom : FunLike (LanguageHom α β) (List α) (List β) where
  coe f l := (f <| FreeMonoid.ofList l).toList
  coe_injective f g h := by ext x; simpa using congr_fun h [x]

def LanguageHom.lift (f : α → List β) (l : List α) := FreeMonoid.lift (FreeMonoid.ofList ∘ f) l

lemma LanguageHom.lift_eq (f : α → List β) (l : List α) : LanguageHom.lift f l = l.flatMap f := by
  simp [lift, ←Function.comp_assoc]
  rfl

But in your scheme the following doesn't type-check:

def LanguageHom.lift' (f : α → List β) : LanguageHom α β :=
  fun (l : List α) ↦ FreeMonoid.lift (FreeMonoid.ofList ∘ f) l

Nor does this:

def LanguageHom.lift'' (f : α → List β) : FreeMonoid α →* FreeMonoid β :=
  fun (l : List α) ↦ FreeMonoid.lift (FreeMonoid.ofList ∘ f) l

because the type of LanguageHom.lift (f : α → List β) is List α → List β. How do I express that LanguageHom.lift (f : α → List β) is in fact a language homomorphism and hence has the properties map_one and map_mul? Note that in my latest approach, I do prove that lift f : List α →* List β and hence lift f will have properties map_one and map_mul (and other API theorems about language homomorphisms I will add).

what i meant above was the the definition of "free monoid" (which is a categorical one) is exactly that monoid homomophisms FreeMonoid α →* M (with M a monoid) are in bijection with ordinary functions α → M via lift, the above applies this to M = FreeMonoid β

It seems to me that the following code is much more straightforward and the reader need not know about free monoids at all. (I apologize for my "Luddite" view, but I'm not sure the categorical view contributes much to the mathematical content here.)

namespace Language

variable {α β : Type*}

scoped instance : MulOne (List α) where
  one := []
  mul := (· ++ ·)

def Hom (α β : Type*) := MonoidHom (List α) (List β)

namespace Hom

theorem map_one (f : List α →* List β) : f [] = [] :=
  MonoidHom.map_one f

theorem map_mul (f : List α →* List β) (as as' : List α) :
    f (as ++ as') = (f as) ++ (f as') :=
  MonoidHom.map_mul f as as'

theorem map_cons (f : List α →* List β) (a : α) (as : List α) :
    f (a :: as) = f [a] ++ f as := by
  rw [← List.singleton_append, map_mul]

def lift (f : α → List β) : List α →* List β where
  toFun := List.flatMap f
  map_one' := List.flatMap_nil
  map_mul' := fun _ _ ↦ List.flatMap_append

theorem lift_map_singleton (f : List α →* List β) :
    lift (fun a ↦ f [a]) = f := by
  ext1 as
  induction as with
  | nil => simp [map_one]
  | cons a as h_ind =>
    rw [map_cons f, ← h_ind]
    simp [lift]

end Hom

end Language

import Mathlib

namespace Language

variable {α β : Type*}

def Hom (α β : Type*) := FreeMonoid α →* FreeMonoid β

instance : FunLike (Hom α β) (List α) (List β) :=
  inferInstanceAs <| FunLike (FreeMonoid α →* FreeMonoid β) (FreeMonoid α) (FreeMonoid β)

def mk (f : List α → List β) (map_nil : f [] = []) (map_append : ∀ a b, f (a ++ b) = f a ++ f b) : Hom α β :=
  { toFun := f
    map_one' := map_nil
    map_mul' := map_append }

  MonoidHom.map_mul f as as'

theorem map_cons (f : Hom α β) (a : α) (as : List α) :
    f (a :: as) = f [a] ++ f as := by
  rw [← List.singleton_append, map_append]

def lift (f : α → List β) : Hom α β :=
  FreeMonoid.lift (show α → FreeMonoid β from f)

@[simp]
theorem lift_singleton (f : α → List β) (a : α) :
    lift f [a] = f a :=
  (FreeMonoid.lift_eval_of (show α → FreeMonoid β from f)) a

theorem lift_map_singleton (f : Hom α β) :
    lift (fun a ↦ f [a]) = f :=
  (FreeMonoid.lift_restrict (show FreeMonoid α →* FreeMonoid β from f))

end Hom

end Language

Mathlib takes the stance that if there are multiple possible instances on a type, then to prefer using Monoid T and Monoid SomeTWrapper to distinguish, rather than using open scoped TheWrapperNamespace. Here's the final code I'm going to use. There is no mention of monoid at all. Should Language be one day refactored to use FreeMonoid, then about half of the code can be replaced by invoking:
https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/FreeMonoid/Basic.html#FreeMonoid.lift
But until that happens, the following code is straightforward and self-contained and should suffice for my purpose. (All I want to do is to prove that regular languages are preserved by image and inverse image operations under homomorphism.)

namespace Language

variable {α β : Type*}

@[ext]
structure Hom (α β : Type*) where
  toFun : List α → List β
  map_nil' : toFun [] = []
  map_append' (as as' : List α) : toFun (as ++ as') = toFun as ++ toFun as'

instance : FunLike (Hom α β) (List α) (List β) where
  coe (f : Hom α β) := f.toFun
  coe_injective (_ _ : Hom α β) := by
    intro _
    ext1
    assumption

namespace Hom

theorem ext_iff' (f f' : Hom α β) :
    f = f' ↔ ∀ as, f as = f' as := by
  constructor
  · grind
  · intro h
    ext1
    ext1 as
    exact h as

theorem map_nil (f : Hom α β) : f [] = [] := f.map_nil'

theorem map_append (f : Hom α β) (as as' : List α) : f (as ++ as') = (f as) ++ (f as') :=
  f.map_append' as as'

theorem map_cons (f : Hom α β) (a : α) (as : List α) :
    f (a :: as) = f [a] ++ f as := by
  rw [← List.singleton_append, map_append]

def liftAux (f : α → List β) : Hom α β where
  toFun := List.flatMap f
  map_nil' := List.flatMap_nil
  map_append' := fun _ _ ↦ List.flatMap_append

theorem liftAux_eq (f : α → List β) : liftAux f = List.flatMap f :=
  rfl

theorem listAux_left_inv (f : α → List β) :
    (fun f a ↦ f [a]) (liftAux f) = f := by
  simp [liftAux_eq]

theorem listAux_right_inv (f : Hom α β) :
    liftAux (fun a ↦ f [a]) = f := by
  rw [ext_iff']
  intro as
  induction as with
  | nil => simp [map_nil]
  | cons a as h_ind =>
    rw [map_cons f, ← h_ind]
    simp [liftAux_eq]

def lift : (α → List β) ≃ (Hom α β) where
  toFun := liftAux
  invFun := fun f a ↦ f [a]
  left_inv := listAux_left_inv
  right_inv := listAux_right_inv

theorem lift_eq (f : α → List β) : lift f = List.flatMap f :=
  rfl

end Hom

end Language
